steps.label: SELECT + WHERE
steps.note: Pick columns, filter rows with WHERE, sort with ORDER BY. Without ORDER BY, row order is not guaranteed.
steps.sql:
SELECT name, city
FROM customers
WHERE city <> 'London'
ORDER BY name;

steps.label: JOIN
steps.note: JOIN matches each order with its customer through the foreign key customer_id → customers.id.
steps.sql:
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
ORDER BY o.id;

steps.label: GROUP BY
steps.note: GROUP BY collapses rows into one per customer; COUNT and SUM work per group.
steps.sql:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders, SUM(o.total) AS spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY spent DESC;

steps.label: LEFT JOIN
steps.note: A LEFT JOIN keeps customers with no orders (Margaret): their order columns are NULL, so COUNT gives 0. An inner JOIN would drop her.
steps.sql:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id
ORDER BY c.id;

steps.label: HAVING
steps.note: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation (all statuses count here).
steps.sql:
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.total) AS spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id
HAVING SUM(o.total) > 30
ORDER BY spent DESC;

steps.label: Subquery
steps.note: A subquery's result feeds the outer query: customers who placed any order over 100.
